title: Ὀδυσσεὺς καὶ Θερσίτης
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Athena’s order has been given, and Odysseus obeys. He throws off his cloak, takes Agamemnon’s ancestral sceptre, and goes along the ships restraining the army: with gentle words for kings and chiefs, with the sceptre and sharp words for common men, and a lesson that the Achaeans cannot all be kings. The men stream back to the assembly with a noise like the sea, and sit down, all but Thersites, an ugly, loud-mouthed man who loves to abuse kings. He attacks Agamemnon for greed and urges the army to sail home. Odysseus answers him sternly, threatens to strip him and beat him from the assembly, and strikes him with the sceptre. Thersites weeps, and the men, grieving as they are, laugh and praise Odysseus.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάθ’, ὃ δὲ ξυνέηκε θεᾶς ὄπα φωνησάσης,
βῆ δὲ θέειν, ἀπὸ δὲ χλαῖναν βάλε· τὴν δὲ κόμισσε
κῆρυξ Εὐρυβάτης Ἰθακήσιος ὅς οἱ ὀπήδει·
sentences.tr:
hōs phath’, ho de xyneēke theas opa phōnēsasēs,
bē de theein, apo de chlainan bale· tēn de komisse
kēryx Eurybatēs Ithakēsios hos hoi opēdei·
sentences.i: So she spoke, and he understood the voice of the goddess who had spoken, and set off running, throwing off his cloak, which the herald Eurybates of Ithaca, who kept him company, took care of;
sentences.n: ὣς φάθ’ is ὣς φάτο ‘so she spoke’ with its last vowel dropped (and τ aspirated before the rough breathing of ὃ), closing Athena’s speech; ὃ δὲ is Odysseus, ‘and he’. ξυνέηκε is the epic aorist of συνίημι (Attic συνῆκε) in its sense ‘take in with the mind, understand’, not the ‘set together’ of 1.8. βῆ δὲ θέειν is ‘he set out to run’, θέειν being the uncontracted θεῖν. ἀπὸ … βάλε is tmesis, ‘threw off’. κόμισσε (κομίζω ‘take care of’) has the epic doubled σ and no augment; ὀπήδει is the imperfect of ὀπηδέω ‘accompany’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ Ἀτρεΐδεω Ἀγαμέμνονος ἀντίος ἐλθὼν
δέξατό οἱ σκῆπτρον πατρώϊον ἄφθιτον αἰεί·
sentences.tr:
autos d’ Atreïdeō Agamemnonos antios elthōn
dexato hoi skēptron patrōïon aphthiton aiei·
sentences.l:
and he himself, having come to meet Atreus’-son Agamemnon,
received from him the sceptre of his fathers, unfailing for ever;
sentences.i: He himself went to meet Agamemnon, son of Atreus, and received from him his fathers’ sceptre, which never fails;
sentences.n: The sceptre is the sign of the right to speak and to command, and the phrase σκῆπτρον πατρώϊον ἄφθιτον αἰεί also ends 2.46, where Agamemnon takes the sceptre up; Odysseus now carries Agamemnon’s authority with him. ἀντίος ἐλθών ‘having come to meet’ takes the genitive Ἀτρεΐδεω Ἀγαμέμνονος (epic -εω for -ου). δέξατό οἱ is ‘received from him’, δέχομαι with the dative οἱ of the giver. ἄφθιτον ‘unfailing’, αἰεί ‘for ever’.

sentences.t: σὺν τῷ ἔβη κατὰ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων.
sentences.tr: syn tōi ebē kata nēas Achaiōn chalkochitōnōn.
sentences.l: with it he went along the ships of the bronze-shirted Achaeans.
sentences.i: With it he went along the ships of the bronze-shirted Achaeans.
sentences.n: σὺν τῷ is ‘with it’: τῷ is the pronoun for the sceptre, not an article. ἔβη ‘he went’, κατὰ νῆας ‘along the ships’, the long row drawn up on the shore. χαλκοχιτώνων ‘bronze-shirted’ is a stock epithet of the Achaeans, translated every time. The line is word for word the one at 2.47, where Agamemnon sets out with the same sceptre.

sentences.t:
ὅν τινα μὲν βασιλῆα καὶ ἔξοχον ἄνδρα κιχείη
τὸν δ’ ἀγανοῖς ἐπέεσσιν ἐρητύσασκε παραστάς·
sentences.tr:
hon tina men basilēa kai exochon andra kicheiē
ton d’ aganois epeessin erētysaske parastas·
sentences.l:
Whatever king, and man standing out, he came upon,
him with gentle words he would restrain, standing beside him:
sentences.i: Whenever he came upon a king or a man who stood out above the rest, he would stand beside him and restrain him with gentle words:
sentences.n: ὅν τινα μὲν … τὸν δ’ is ‘whichever one … him’. The relative clause with the optative κιχείη (κιχάνω ‘come upon’) and the iterative ἐρητύσασκε, whose -σκ- marks repetition, tells of something done again and again: ‘he would restrain’. βασιλῆα is the epic accusative of βασιλεύς, and ἔξοχον ‘standing out’ means above the rest. ἀγανοῖς ἐπέεσσιν ‘with gentle words’ and ἐρητύω ‘restrain’ carry out Athena’s order at 180.

sentences.t:
δαιμόνι’ οὔ σε ἔοικε κακὸν ὣς δειδίσσεσθαι,
ἀλλ’ αὐτός τε κάθησο καὶ ἄλλους ἵδρυε λαούς·
sentences.tr:
daimoni’ ou se eoike kakon hōs deidissesthai,
all’ autos te kathēso kai allous hidrye laous·
sentences.l:
“Strange man, it is not fitting that you be frightened like a coward,
but sit down yourself, and seat the other people;
sentences.i: “Strange man, it does not become you to be frightened like a coward; sit down yourself, and make the rest of the people sit.
sentences.n: δαιμόνιε ‘strange man’ (written δαιμόνι’) is an address whose force is not settled: it can be gentle or scolding, and here a king is being coaxed. οὔ σε ἔοικε is ‘it is not fitting for you’. κακὸν ὣς is ‘like a κακός’, a man without courage; δειδίσσεσθαι is a rare epic form of the verb of fear, taken here as ‘to be frightened’. κάθησο is the imperative of κάθημαι ‘sit’, and ἵδρυε the imperative of ἱδρύω ‘make sit, settle’. λαούς is the accusative plural of λαός ‘people’.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ πω σάφα οἶσθ’ οἷος νόος Ἀτρεΐωνος·
sentences.tr: ou gar pō sapha oisth’ hoios noos Atreïōnos·
sentences.l: for not yet clearly do you know what the mind is of Atreus’-son;
sentences.i: for you do not yet know clearly what the mind of the son of Atreus is;
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ ‘for not’ gives the reason for staying calm: the king’s purpose is not yet clear. οἶσθ’ is οἶσθα ‘you know’, οἷος ‘of what sort’ (an indirect question), and νόος the uncontracted νοῦς ‘mind’. Ἀτρεΐωνος is the genitive of Ἀτρεΐων, a patronymic like Ἀτρεΐδης, ‘son of Atreus’.

sentences.t: νῦν μὲν πειρᾶται, τάχα δ’ ἴψεται υἷας Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr: nyn men peiratai, tacha d’ ipsetai huias Achaiōn.
sentences.l: now he is making trial, but soon he will strike hard the sons of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: Now he is only making trial of them, but soon he will strike the sons of the Achaeans hard.
sentences.n: νῦν μὲν … τάχα δ’ sets ‘now’ against ‘soon’. πειρᾶται is πειράω ‘make trial of’, the test of the army that Agamemnon announced at 2.73. ἴψεται is the future of ἴπτω ‘strike hard’, a rare verb kept with its traditional sense (compare ἴψαο at 1.454). υἷας is the Ionic accusative plural of υἱός.

sentences.t: ἐν βουλῇ δ’ οὐ πάντες ἀκούσαμεν οἷον ἔειπε.
sentences.tr: en boulēi d’ ou pantes akousamen hoion eeipe.
sentences.l: And in the council not all of us heard what sort of thing he said.
sentences.i: And in the council we did not all hear what he said.
sentences.n: ἐν βουλῇ ‘in the council’ looks back to the meeting of the chiefs at the start of this book; οὐ πάντες ‘not all’ is as far as Odysseus goes, and he does not say who did not hear. ἀκούσαμεν is the aorist ‘we heard’, and οἷον ἔειπε an indirect exclamation, ‘what sort of thing he said’, with ἔειπε the epic aorist of εἶπον.

sentences.t: μή τι χολωσάμενος ῥέξῃ κακὸν υἷας Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.tr: mē ti cholōsamenos rhexēi kakon huias Achaiōn·
sentences.l: lest, having been angered, he do some evil to the sons of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: for fear that in his anger he may do some harm to the sons of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: μή τι … ῥέξῃ is the construction of fear or warning, μή with the subjunctive: ‘lest he should do’. χολωσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of χολόομαι ‘become angry’ (χολόω ‘make angry’, from χόλος ‘anger’); ῥέξῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ῥέζω ‘do’, and κακὸν ῥέξαι ‘do evil’ is a stock phrase. υἷας Ἀχαιῶν ‘the sons of the Achaeans’ repeats the end of 193.

sentences.t:
θυμὸς δὲ μέγας ἐστὶ διοτρεφέων βασιλήων,
τιμὴ δ’ ἐκ Διός ἐστι, φιλεῖ δέ ἑ μητίετα Ζεύς.
sentences.tr:
thymos de megas esti diotrepheōn basilēōn,
timē d’ ek Dios esti, philei de he mētieta Zeus.
sentences.l:
and great is the heart of Zeus-nurtured kings,
and honour is from Zeus, and him loves counsellor Zeus.”
sentences.i: The heart of Zeus-nurtured kings is great; their honour comes from Zeus, and Zeus the counsellor loves each of them.”
sentences.n: θυμὸς μέγας is the great heart of pride and temper: Odysseus warns that kings are dangerous to cross. διοτρεφέων is the epic genitive plural of διοτρεφής ‘Zeus-nurtured’, a stock epithet of kings, translated every time. τιμή is the king’s ‘honour’, his standing, which comes ἐκ Διός ‘from Zeus’. ἑ is the pronoun ‘him’ (the king in general), so the English says ‘each of them’. μητίετα (epic -α for -ης) ‘counsellor’ is Zeus’s epithet.

sentences.t:
ὃν δ’ αὖ δήμου τ’ ἄνδρα ἴδοι βοόωντά τ’ ἐφεύροι,
τὸν σκήπτρῳ ἐλάσασκεν ὁμοκλήσασκέ τε μύθῳ·
sentences.tr:
hon d’ au dēmou t’ andra idoi booōnta t’ epheuroi,
ton skēptrōi elasasken homoklēsaske te mythōi·
sentences.l:
But in turn, whatever man of the people he saw, and found shouting,
him with the sceptre he would strike, and rebuke with a word:
sentences.i: But whenever he saw a man of the people shouting, and found him at it, he would strike him with the sceptre and rebuke him with a word:
sentences.n: ὃν δ’ αὖ … answers ὅν τινα μὲν at 188: first the kings, now the common men. δήμου ἄνδρα is ‘a man of the people’, the ordinary soldier; βοόωντα is βοάω ‘shout’ uncontracted. ἴδοι and ἐφεύροι (ἐφευρίσκω ‘find’) are optatives, and ἐλάσασκεν (ἐλαύνω ‘drive, strike’) and ὁμοκλήσασκε (ὁμοκλάω ‘rebuke sharply’) are iteratives again: all this was done repeatedly. The sceptre becomes a staff for striking, as it does on Thersites at 265.

sentences.t:
δαιμόνι’ ἀτρέμας ἧσο καὶ ἄλλων μῦθον ἄκουε,
οἳ σέο φέρτεροί εἰσι, σὺ δ’ ἀπτόλεμος καὶ ἄναλκις
οὔτέ ποτ’ ἐν πολέμῳ ἐναρίθμιος οὔτ’ ἐνὶ βουλῇ·
sentences.tr:
daimoni’ atremas hēso kai allōn mython akoue,
hoi seo pherteroi eisi, sy d’ aptolemos kai analkis
oute pot’ en polemōi enarithmios out’ eni boulēi·
sentences.i: “Strange man, sit still and listen to what others say, who are stronger than you; you are unwarlike and without might, and of no account either in war or in council.
sentences.n: The same address δαιμόνιε as in 190, to a different hearer, and a much harder tone than the one used on the kings. ἧσο is the imperative of ἧμαι ‘sit’, and ἀτρέμας ‘without moving’. σέο is the epic genitive of σύ, ‘than you’, with φέρτεροι ‘stronger’, a comparative meaning superior in power or rank. ἀπτόλεμος is ‘not fit for war’ (πτόλεμος = πόλεμος), ἄναλκις ‘without ἀλκή, defensive strength’, and ἐναρίθμιος ‘counted in the number’.
sentences.mark: Odysseus speaks to a common man

sentences.t: οὐ μέν πως πάντες βασιλεύσομεν ἐνθάδ’ Ἀχαιοί·
sentences.tr: ou men pōs pantes basileusomen enthad’ Achaioi·
sentences.l: In no way, truly, shall we all be kings here, we Achaeans;
sentences.i: We Achaeans cannot all be kings here;
sentences.n: οὐ μέν πως is ‘by no means, truly’. βασιλεύσομεν is the future of βασιλεύω ‘be king’, ἐνθάδ’ is ‘here’, and πάντες … Ἀχαιοί, ‘all of us Achaeans’, wraps round the verb. Odysseus passes from the man’s uselessness to the principle: authority cannot be shared out.

sentences.t: οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη·
sentences.tr: ouk agathon polykoiraniē·
sentences.l: not good is many-rulership;
sentences.i: Rule by many is no good;
sentences.n: πολυκοιρανίη is a compound made from πολύς ‘many’ and κοίρανος ‘ruler’, with the Ionic ending -ίη for -ία: ‘the rule of many lords’. The verb is left out (‘[is] not good’), as in a maxim. κοίρανος ‘ruler’ returns in the next words.

sentences.t:
εἷς κοίρανος ἔστω,
εἷς βασιλεύς, ᾧ δῶκε Κρόνου πάϊς ἀγκυλομήτεω
σκῆπτρόν τ’ ἠδὲ θέμιστας, ἵνά σφισι βουλεύῃσι.
sentences.tr:
heis koiranos estō,
heis basileus, hōi dōke Kronou païs ankylomēteō
skēptron t’ ēde themistas, hina sphisi bouleuēisi.
sentences.i: Let there be one ruler, one king, to whom the son of Cronus, of crooked cunning, has given the sceptre and the ordinances, so that he may take counsel for them.”
sentences.n: ἔστω is the imperative ‘let there be’, and ᾧ the relative ‘to whom’. ἀγκυλομήτεω is the epic genitive of ἀγκυλομήτης and agrees with Κρόνου: the epithet belongs to Cronus, ‘of crooked cunning’ (ἀγκύλος ‘curved’ and μῆτις ‘cunning’; the exact sense is uncertain). Κρόνου πάϊς ‘child of Cronus’ is Zeus. θέμιστας ‘ordinances’ are the king’s rulings and customary rights. σφισι is ‘for them’, the army; βουλεύῃσι is a subjunctive with the longer ending -σι.

sentences.t: ὣς ὅ γε κοιρανέων δίεπε στρατόν·
sentences.tr: hōs ho ge koiraneōn diepe straton·
sentences.l: Thus he, acting as ruler, set the army in order;
sentences.i: So he went through the army as its ruler, setting it in order;
sentences.n: ὣς ὅ γε is ‘so he’. κοιρανέων is the participle of κοιρανέω ‘act as κοίρανος, ruler’ and takes up κοίρανος at 204: Odysseus does what he has just preached. δίεπε is the imperfect of διέπω ‘manage, order’, with no augment. The sentence breaks off at the ano teleia in mid-line, and the next unit has the men on the move.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἀγορὴν δὲ
αὖτις ἐπεσσεύοντο νεῶν ἄπο καὶ κλισιάων
ἠχῇ, ὡς ὅτε κῦμα πολυφλοίσβοιο θαλάσσης
αἰγιαλῷ μεγάλῳ βρέμεται, σμαραγεῖ δέ τε πόντος.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ agorēn de
autis epesseuonto neōn apo kai klisiaōn
ēchēi, hōs hote kyma polyphloisboio thalassēs
aigialōi megalōi bremetai, smaragei de te pontos.
sentences.l:
and they to the assembly
back again rushed from the ships and the huts
with a din, as when a wave of the much-roaring sea
on the great beach booms, and the open sea resounds.
sentences.i: and they rushed back to the assembly from the ships and the huts with a din, as when a wave of the loud-roaring sea booms on a great beach and the open sea resounds.
sentences.n: The army streams back. ἀγορὴν δὲ is ἀγορήν with the suffix -δε, ‘to the assembly’ (two words in print). ἐπεσσεύοντο is the imperfect of ἐπισεύομαι ‘rush to’, with the epic doubled σ; νεῶν ἄπο is ἀπὸ νεῶν with the preposition after its noun; κλισιάων is the epic genitive plural of κλισίη ‘hut’. ἠχῇ ‘with a din’ opens a simile, ὡς ὅτε ‘as when’. πολυφλοίσβοιο is a stock epithet of the sea, ‘much-roaring’ in the literal line and ‘loud-roaring’ in the free one, translated every time; σμαραγεῖ is the verb of a deep roar.

sentences.t: ἄλλοι μέν ῥ’ ἕζοντο, ἐρήτυθεν δὲ καθ’ ἕδρας·
sentences.tr: alloi men rh’ hezonto, erētythen de kath’ hedras·
sentences.l: The others, then, sat down, and were restrained to their seats;
sentences.i: The others sat down and were restrained in their seats;
sentences.n: ἄλλοι μέν ῥ’ ἕζοντο ‘the others then sat down’ is answered by the single man of the next line. ῥ’ is ῥα (ἄρα) ‘then’. ἐρήτυθεν is the passive aorist of ἐρητύω ‘restrain’, with -εν for -ησαν, the verb of 164, 180 and 189. καθ’ ἕδρας is ‘down to their seats’. The edition’s paragraph break here marks the start of the Thersites episode.

sentences.t: Θερσίτης δ’ ἔτι μοῦνος ἀμετροεπὴς ἐκολῴα,
sentences.tr: Thersitēs d’ eti mounos ametroepēs ekolōia,
sentences.l: And Thersites, still alone, of unmeasured words, kept up his brawling,
sentences.i: Only Thersites, a man with no measure in his speech, still kept up his clamour,
sentences.n: Θερσίτης seems to be built on θέρσος, the Aeolic form of θάρσος ‘boldness’ (probable, not certain). ἔτι μοῦνος is ‘still alone’ (μοῦνος = μόνος). ἀμετροεπής is ἄμετρος ‘without measure’ and ἔπος ‘word’. ἐκολῴα is the imperfect of κολῳάω ‘brawl, make an uproar’, the verb of κολῳός at 1.575.

sentences.t:
ὃς ἔπεα φρεσὶν ᾗσιν ἄκοσμά τε πολλά τε ᾔδη
μάψ, ἀτὰρ οὐ κατὰ κόσμον, ἐριζέμεναι βασιλεῦσιν,
ἀλλ’ ὅ τι οἱ εἴσαιτο γελοίϊον Ἀργείοισιν
ἔμμεναι·
sentences.tr:
hos epea phresin hēisin akosma te polla te ēidē
maps, atar ou kata kosmon, erizemenai basileusin,
all’ ho ti hoi eisaito geloiïon Argeioisin
emmenai·
sentences.l:
who words in his mind, disorderly and many, knew,
rashly, and not in due order, to quarrel with kings,
but whatever might seem to him laughable to the Argives
to be;
sentences.i: who knew many disorderly words in his mind, for quarrelling with kings, rashly and not in due order, and whatever seemed to him laughable to the Argives;
sentences.n: ᾔδη is the pluperfect of οἶδα, ‘he knew’ (Attic ᾔδει). ἔπεα … ἄκοσμά τε πολλά τε is ‘words, disorderly and many’, ἄκοσμα ‘without order’ echoing οὐ κατὰ κόσμον ‘not in due order’. ἐριζέμεναι (ἐρίζω ‘quarrel’) is an infinitive of purpose, with the dative βασιλεῦσιν. ἀλλ’ ὅ τι … names the other kind of word he knew: εἴσαιτο is the aorist optative of εἴδομαι ‘seem’, with οἱ ‘to him’ and ἔμμεναι the epic ‘to be’; γελοίϊον Ἀργείοισιν is ‘laughable to the Argives’.

sentences.t: αἴσχιστος δὲ ἀνὴρ ὑπὸ Ἴλιον ἦλθε·
sentences.tr: aischistos de anēr hypo Ilion ēlthe·
sentences.l: and ugliest man to Ilium came;
sentences.i: He was the ugliest man who came to Ilium;
sentences.n: αἴσχιστος is the superlative of αἰσχρός, a word that covers ‘ugly’ and ‘shameful’; what follows describes the body, from the feet up. ὑπὸ Ἴλιον is ‘to Ilium’, ὑπό with the accusative meaning ‘up under’ the walls. ἦλθε is the aorist ‘came’.

sentences.t: φολκὸς ἔην, χωλὸς δ’ ἕτερον πόδα·
sentences.tr: pholkos eēn, chōlos d’ heteron poda·
sentences.l: He was bandy-legged, and lame as to one foot;
sentences.i: He was bandy-legged, and lame in one foot;
sentences.n: The meaning of φολκός is not known. ‘Bandy-legged’ is the usual guess and ‘squint-eyed’ the other ancient one; the translation takes the first. ἔην is the epic imperfect of εἰμί (Attic ἦν). χωλὸς δ’ ἕτερον πόδα is ‘lame as to the one foot’, πόδα an accusative of respect; ἕτερον marks one of the pair, and the Greek does not say which.

sentences.t:
τὼ δέ οἱ ὤμω
κυρτὼ ἐπὶ στῆθος συνοχωκότε·
sentences.tr:
tō de hoi ōmō
kyrtō epi stēthos synochōkote·
sentences.l:
and his two shoulders
hunched, drawn together over his chest;
sentences.i: and his two shoulders were humped, drawn together over his chest;
sentences.n: Three duals in a row: τὼ … ὤμω ‘the two shoulders’ (τὼ is the dual article), κυρτὼ ‘humped’, and συνοχωκότε, the perfect participle of συνέχω ‘hold together, draw together’. οἱ is ‘his’, a dative of the person. ἐπὶ στῆθος is ‘towards the chest’: the shoulders curve in over it.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὕπερθε
φοξὸς ἔην κεφαλήν, ψεδνὴ δ’ ἐπενήνοθε λάχνη.
sentences.tr:
autar hyperthe
phoxos eēn kephalēn, psednē d’ epenēnothe lachnē.
sentences.l:
and above
peaked he was in the head, and sparse down grew upon it.
sentences.i: and above, his head came to a point, and sparse down grew on it.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὕπερθε ‘and above’ moves the portrait to the head. φοξός ‘pointed, peaked’ is a rare word, and this is its usual explanation; κεφαλήν is an accusative of respect, ‘in the head’. ψεδνή ‘thin, sparse’ goes with λάχνη ‘down, wool’. ἐπενήνοθε is a perfect with present sense, from a rare verb, taken as ‘grows upon’.

sentences.t: ἔχθιστος δ’ Ἀχιλῆϊ μάλιστ’ ἦν ἠδ’ Ὀδυσῆϊ·
sentences.tr: echthistos d’ Achilēï malist’ ēn ēd’ Odysēï·
sentences.l: Most hateful was he to Achilles above all and to Odysseus;
sentences.i: He was most hateful of all to Achilles and to Odysseus;
sentences.n: ἔχθιστος is the superlative of ἐχθρός ‘hateful, hated’, and the datives Ἀχιλῆϊ … Ὀδυσῆϊ name the two who hated him; μάλιστ’ ‘most of all’ strengthens it. Ὀδυσῆϊ is the epic dative with a single σ, while the name has σσ in Ὀδυσσεύς at 244: both spellings serve the metre.

sentences.t: τὼ γὰρ νεικείεσκε·
sentences.tr: tō gar neikeieske·
sentences.l: for those two he used to rebuke;
sentences.i: for he used to rebuke those two;
sentences.n: τὼ is the dual ‘those two’, Achilles and Odysseus, and γάρ explains why they hated him. νεικείεσκε is an iterative imperfect of νεικέω ‘rebuke’; the -σκ- shows repetition, ‘he used to rebuke’. The Greek verb is strong, covering abuse and quarrelling, but ‘rebuke’ is kept as its rendering throughout.

sentences.t:
τότ’ αὖτ’ Ἀγαμέμνονι δίῳ
ὀξέα κεκλήγων λέγ’ ὀνείδεα·
sentences.tr:
tot’ aut’ Agamemnoni diōi
oxea keklēgōn leg’ oneidea·
sentences.l:
this time, in turn, at heavenly Agamemnon
shrilly shrieking, he spoke out reproaches;
sentences.i: this time, in his turn, he shrilly screamed out reproaches at heavenly Agamemnon;
sentences.n: τότ’ αὖτ’ ‘then in turn’ is ‘this time’. κεκλήγων is the perfect participle of κλάζω ‘shriek’, the verb for the rattle of Apollo’s arrows at 1.46; ὀξέα is taken as an adverb, ‘shrilly’. λέγ’ is λέγε, the unaugmented imperfect of λέγω ‘recount’; ὀνείδεα ‘reproaches’ is the uncontracted neuter plural. Ἀγαμέμνονι δίῳ ‘heavenly Agamemnon’ has the stock epithet δῖος, translated every time.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἄρ’ Ἀχαιοὶ
ἐκπάγλως κοτέοντο νεμέσσηθέν τ’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ.
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ ar’ Achaioi
ekpaglōs koteonto nemessēthen t’ eni thymōi.
sentences.l:
and at him the Achaeans
terribly bore a grudge, and felt resentment in their heart.
sentences.i: The Achaeans terribly bore him a grudge, and felt resentment in their hearts.
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘at him’, the dative with κοτέω ‘bear a grudge’: the Achaeans are angry with Thersites, not with the king. ἐκπάγλως ‘terribly’. κοτέοντο is imperfect, and νεμέσσηθεν the passive aorist (-εν for -ησαν) of νεμεσσάω ‘feel resentment’. ἐνὶ θυμῷ ‘in their heart’ is singular for the whole army.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὃ μακρὰ βοῶν Ἀγαμέμνονα νείκεε μύθῳ·
sentences.tr: autar ho makra boōn Agamemnona neikee mythōi·
sentences.l: And he, crying out loudly, rebuked Agamemnon with a word:
sentences.i: And he, shouting loudly, rebuked Agamemnon in these words:
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὃ: ὃ is ‘he’, Thersites. μακρὰ βοῶν ‘crying out loudly’: βοῶν is the participle of βοάω ‘shout’, and μακρά, literally ‘long’, is a neuter plural used as an adverb. νείκεε is the unaugmented imperfect of νεικέω ‘rebuke’, and μύθῳ ‘with a word’ the dative of means. The line introduces Thersites’ speech, which runs to 242.

sentences.t: Ἀτρεΐδη τέο δ’ αὖτ’ ἐπιμέμφεαι ἠδὲ χατίζεις;
sentences.tr: Atreïdē teo d’ aut’ epimempheai ēde chatizeis;
sentences.l: “Atreus’-son, of what again do you find fault, and what do you lack?
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, what is it that you are finding fault with now, and what do you lack?
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδη is the vocative ‘Son of Atreus’. Thersites’ speech echoes Achilles’ quarrel in book 1, and two of its lines, 240 and 242, are Achilles’ own. τέο is the epic genitive of τίς ‘of what?’ and serves both verbs, which take the genitive: ἐπιμέμφεαι (= ἐπιμέμφῃ, ‘you find fault with’) and χατίζεις ‘you need, you lack’. αὖτ’ is ‘again’.

sentences.t:
πλεῖαί τοι χαλκοῦ κλισίαι, πολλαὶ δὲ γυναῖκες
εἰσὶν ἐνὶ κλισίῃς ἐξαίρετοι, ἅς τοι Ἀχαιοὶ
πρωτίστῳ δίδομεν εὖτ’ ἂν πτολίεθρον ἕλωμεν.
sentences.tr:
pleiai toi chalkou klisiai, pollai de gynaikes
eisin eni klisiēis exairetoi, has toi Achaioi
prōtistōi didomen eut’ an ptoliethron helōmen.
sentences.l:
Full of bronze are your huts, and many women
are in your huts, picked out, whom to you we Achaeans
first of all give, whenever we take a citadel.
sentences.i: Your huts are full of bronze, and in your huts are many women, picked out for you, whom we Achaeans give to you first of all whenever we take a citadel.
sentences.n: πλεῖαι is the epic feminine plural ‘full’ (Attic πλέαι); τοι (= σοι) is ‘for you’, and χαλκοῦ the genitive of what fills them. ἐξαίρετοι ‘picked out’ means chosen from the spoil before the rest. πρωτίστῳ is a dative superlative, ‘to you, the foremost’. εὖτ’ ἂν … ἕλωμεν is ‘whenever we take’, ἕλωμεν the aorist subjunctive of αἱρέω. The best prizes go to the king first: that is the grievance.

sentences.t:
ἦ ἔτι καὶ χρυσοῦ ἐπιδεύεαι, ὅν κέ τις οἴσει
Τρώων ἱπποδάμων ἐξ Ἰλίου υἷος ἄποινα,
ὅν κεν ἐγὼ δήσας ἀγάγω ἢ ἄλλος Ἀχαιῶν,
sentences.tr:
ē eti kai chrysou epideueai, hon ke tis oisei
Trōōn hippodamōn ex Iliou huios apoina,
hon ken egō dēsas agagō ē allos Achaiōn,
sentences.l:
Or do you still want gold also, which someone will bring
of the horse-taming Trojans from Ilium as ransom for a son,
whom I, having bound him, may lead in, or another of the Achaeans,
sentences.i: Or do you still need gold as well, gold that one of the Trojans, those tamers of horses, will bring from Ilium as ransom for a son, a son whom I, or some other Achaean, may bind and lead in,
sentences.n: ἦ opens the question, ‘or …?’, and ἔτι καὶ is ‘still … as well’; ἐπιδεύεαι (= ἐπιδεύῃ) is ‘you are in want of’, with the genitive χρυσοῦ. The first ὅν is the gold, ὅν κέ τις οἴσει ‘which someone will bring’ (οἴσει, future of φέρω); the second ὅν is the son, and υἷος is the genitive ‘for a son’ with ἄποινα ‘ransom’. ἀγάγω is the aorist subjunctive of ἄγω ‘lead’. ἱπποδάμων ‘horse-taming’ is a stock epithet of the Trojans, translated every time.

sentences.t:
ἠὲ γυναῖκα νέην, ἵνα μίσγεαι ἐν φιλότητι,
ἥν τ’ αὐτὸς ἀπονόσφι κατίσχεαι;
sentences.tr:
ēe gynaika neēn, hina misgeai en philotēti,
hēn t’ autos aponosphi katischeai;
sentences.l:
or a young woman, that you may mingle with her in love,
whom you yourself will keep back apart?
sentences.i: Or a young woman, that you may lie with her in love, and keep her apart for yourself?
sentences.n: ἠέ ‘or’ brings a second thing Agamemnon may want. μίσγεαι and κατίσχεαι are second-person subjunctives in -εαι (= -ῃ), middle: μίσγομαι ‘mingle with’ and κατίσχομαι (= κατέχω) ‘hold back’ for oneself. ἵνα μίσγεαι ἐν φιλότητι ‘that you may mingle in love’ is the language of sexual union, and ἀπονόσφι ‘apart’ means he keeps her to himself, away from the other men. The question ends at the Greek question mark in mid-line.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν ἔοικεν
ἀρχὸν ἐόντα κακῶν ἐπιβασκέμεν υἷας Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
ou men eoiken
archon eonta kakōn epibaskemen huias Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
It is truly not fitting
for one who is a commander to bring the sons of the Achaeans into evils.
sentences.i: It is not right that a commander should lead the sons of the Achaeans into evils.
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν ἔοικεν ‘it is truly not fitting’ uses the same ἔοικε as Odysseus at 190. ἀρχὸν ἐόντα is ‘being a commander’ (ἀρχός, with ἐόντα the epic participle of εἰμί), agreeing with an unspoken ‘you’. ἐπιβασκέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἐπιβάσκω, the causative of ἐπιβαίνω ‘step on’: ‘to make go upon’, and the genitive κακῶν gives the place, ‘into evils’. υἷας Ἀχαιῶν as in 195.

sentences.t:
ὦ πέπονες κάκ’ ἐλέγχε’ Ἀχαιΐδες οὐκέτ’ Ἀχαιοὶ
οἴκαδέ περ σὺν νηυσὶ νεώμεθα, τόνδε δ’ ἐῶμεν
αὐτοῦ ἐνὶ Τροίῃ γέρα πεσσέμεν, ὄφρα ἴδηται
ἤ ῥά τί οἱ χἠμεῖς προσαμύνομεν ἦε καὶ οὐκί·
sentences.tr:
ō pepones kak’ elenche’ Achaiïdes ouket’ Achaioi
oikade per syn nēusi neōmetha, tonde d’ eōmen
autou eni Troiēi gera pessemen, ophra idētai
ē rha ti hoi chēmeis prosamynomen ēe kai ouki·
sentences.l:
O good ones, base reproaches, Achaean women, no longer Achaeans,
let us go home indeed with our ships, and let us leave this man
there in Troy to digest his prizes, so that he may see
whether we too are of any help to him, or not;
sentences.i: My good fellows, base disgraces, Achaean women and no longer Achaean men, let us go home with our ships, and leave this man here in Troy to digest his prizes of honour, so that he may see whether we too are any help to him, or not;
sentences.n: ὦ πέπονες: the meaning of πέπων is not known (‘soft’ or ‘ripe’ is the usual guess), and said to a crowd of men it is read here as scornful. κάκ’ ἐλέγχε’ is κακὰ ἐλέγχεα ‘base disgraces’, a nominative used as an insult; Ἀχαιΐδες is ‘Achaean women’. νεώμεθα and ἐῶμεν are hortatory subjunctives, ‘let us go’, ‘let us leave’. πεσσέμεν (= πέσσειν) is ‘to cook, to digest’: let him sit over his prizes. ὄφρα ἴδηται gives the purpose; χἠμεῖς is καὶ ἡμεῖς ‘we too’; προσαμύνομεν ‘we help’.

sentences.t:
ὃς καὶ νῦν Ἀχιλῆα ἕο μέγ’ ἀμείνονα φῶτα
ἠτίμησεν· ἑλὼν γὰρ ἔχει γέρας αὐτὸς ἀπούρας.
sentences.tr:
hos kai nyn Achilēa heo meg’ ameinona phōta
ētimēsen· helōn gar echei geras autos apouras.
sentences.l:
who even now Achilles, than himself much better a man,
has dishonoured; for he has taken and holds the prize, himself having taken it away.
sentences.i: He has even now dishonoured Achilles, a man far better than himself; for he has taken his prize of honour and keeps it, having seized it himself.
sentences.n: ὃς καί is ‘who even’, the relative taking up τόνδε ‘this man’, Agamemnon. ἕο is the epic genitive of the reflexive pronoun, ‘than himself’, the genitive of comparison after ἀμείνονα ‘better’; μέγ’ is ‘much’, and φῶτα ‘man’. Line 240 is word for word Achilles’ own line at 1.356, where he said it of Agamemnon; Thersites throws it back at the king. ἑλὼν … ἀπούρας are two aorist participles, ‘having taken … having taken away’ (ἀπαυράω), with ἔχει ‘holds’; αὐτός ‘himself’ puts the act on Agamemnon alone, and γέρας is the prize of honour. Thersites takes Achilles’ side only in order to attack the king.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ μάλ’ οὐκ Ἀχιλῆϊ χόλος φρεσίν, ἀλλὰ μεθήμων·
ἦ γὰρ ἂν Ἀτρεΐδη νῦν ὕστατα λωβήσαιο·
sentences.tr:
alla mal’ ouk Achilēï cholos phresin, alla methēmōn·
ē gar an Atreïdē nyn hystata lōbēsaio·
sentences.l:
But indeed there is no anger in Achilles’ mind, but he is slack;
for truly, Atreus’-son, now for the last time you would do outrage.”
sentences.i: But really there is no anger in Achilles’ mind; he is slack. For truly, son of Atreus, this would now be the last outrage you committed.”
sentences.n: Thersites says Achilles is not angry enough to act; if he were, Agamemnon’s outrage would now be his last. μεθήμων ‘slack, remiss’ is the adjective of μεθίημι ‘let go’, and ἀλλὰ μάλ’ is ‘but truly’. Line 242 is Achilles’ own threat from 1.232: ἦ γὰρ ἂν … λωβήσαιο is ἄν with the aorist optative, ‘you would do outrage’, and Thersites reuses it.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο νεικείων Ἀγαμέμνονα ποιμένα λαῶν,
Θερσίτης·
sentences.tr:
hōs phato neikeiōn Agamemnona poimena laōn,
Thersitēs·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, rebuking Agamemnon, shepherd of the people,
Thersites;
sentences.i: So Thersites spoke, rebuking Agamemnon, shepherd of the people;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’ closes the speech; φάτο is the unaugmented aorist of φημί. νεικείων is the participle of νεικέω ‘rebuke’; ποιμένα λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is a stock epithet of Agamemnon, translated every time. The name Θερσίτης is held back to the start of the next line, so that the sentence ends on the speaker.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ὦκα παρίστατο δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
καί μιν ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν χαλεπῷ ἠνίπαπε μύθῳ·
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ ōka paristato dios Odysseus,
kai min hypodra idōn chalepōi ēnipape mythōi·
sentences.l:
and beside him quickly stood heavenly Odysseus,
and with a scowl looking at him, with a harsh word rebuked him:
sentences.i: Heavenly Odysseus quickly stood beside him and, looking at him with a scowl, rebuked him with a harsh word:
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘beside him’, the dative with παρίστατο (παρίσταμαι ‘stand beside’), and ὦκα ‘quickly’. δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς ‘heavenly Odysseus’ has the stock epithet δῖος, translated every time. ὑπόδρα ἰδών is ‘looking with a scowl’, literally ‘from under’ the brows, by the ancient explanation. ἠνίπαπε is the reduplicated aorist of ἐνίπτω ‘rebuke’, with χαλεπῷ … μύθῳ ‘a harsh word’. Odysseus now does to Thersites what 198–199 told of the common men.

sentences.t:
Θερσῖτ’ ἀκριτόμυθε, λιγύς περ ἐὼν ἀγορητής,
ἴσχεο, μηδ’ ἔθελ’ οἶος ἐριζέμεναι βασιλεῦσιν·
sentences.tr:
Thersit’ akritomythe, ligys per eōn agorētēs,
ischeo, mēd’ ethel’ oios erizemenai basileusin·
sentences.l:
“Thersites, of unsorted speech, though you are a clear-voiced speaker,
hold yourself back, and do not wish alone to quarrel with kings;
sentences.i: “Thersites, you who speak without sorting your words, clear-voiced speaker though you are, hold yourself back, and do not try, alone as you are, to quarrel with kings;
sentences.n: Θερσῖτ’ is the vocative. ἀκριτόμυθε is ἄκριτος and μῦθος; ἄκριτος can mean ‘unsorted’, ‘confused’ or ‘endless’, and the exact sense is not known, so the translation takes the plainest, ‘of unsorted speech’. λιγύς περ ἐών is ‘though you are clear-voiced’, and ἀγορητής ‘speaker’ in the assembly. ἴσχεο is the middle imperative of ἴσχω ‘hold yourself back’; ἔθελ’ is ἔθελε ‘be willing’; οἶος ‘alone’; ἐριζέμεναι as at 214.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἐγὼ σέο φημὶ χερειότερον βροτὸν ἄλλον
ἔμμεναι, ὅσσοι ἅμ’ Ἀτρεΐδῃς ὑπὸ Ἴλιον ἦλθον.
sentences.tr:
ou gar egō seo phēmi chereioteron broton allon
emmenai, hossoi ham’ Atreïdēis hypo Ilion ēlthon.
sentences.l:
For I say there is no other mortal worse than you
of all who with the sons of Atreus came to Ilium.
sentences.i: For I say that no other mortal is worse than you, of all who came with the sons of Atreus to Ilium.
sentences.n: χερειότερον is the comparative of χέρης ‘inferior’, here ‘worse’; with σέο (the epic genitive of σύ, ‘than you’) it is the opposite of ἀμείνονα in 239. φημὶ … ἔμμεναι is ‘I say … to be’, with βροτὸν ἄλλον ‘another mortal’ as its subject. ὅσσοι is ‘as many as’. Ἀτρεΐδῃς is a rare dative plural, ‘with the sons of Atreus’, Agamemnon and Menelaus.

sentences.t:
τὼ οὐκ ἂν βασιλῆας ἀνὰ στόμ’ ἔχων ἀγορεύοις,
καί σφιν ὀνείδεά τε προφέροις, νόστόν τε φυλάσσοις.
sentences.tr:
tō ouk an basilēas ana stom’ echōn agoreuois,
kai sphin oneidea te propherois, noston te phylassois.
sentences.l:
Therefore you should not, with kings in your mouth, declare,
and hurl reproaches at them, and keep watch for homecoming.
sentences.i: So you should not declaim with kings on your lips, hurl reproaches at them and keep watch for your homecoming.
sentences.n: τὼ (= τῷ) is ‘therefore’. The optatives ἀγορεύοις, προφέροις and φυλάσσοις all stand under οὐκ ἂν: ‘you should not …’, a mild prohibition. ἀνὰ στόμ’ ἔχων is ‘having (the kings) in your mouth’, that is, talking of them all the time. προφέροις is ‘bring forward against’, with ὀνείδεα ‘reproaches’; νόστον … φυλάσσοις ‘watch for the homecoming’ mocks the wish to go home that Thersites voiced at 236.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τί πω σάφα ἴδμεν ὅπως ἔσται τάδε ἔργα,
ἢ εὖ ἦε κακῶς νοστήσομεν υἷες Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
oude ti pō sapha idmen hopōs estai tade erga,
ē eu ēe kakōs nostēsomen huies Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
Nor do we yet clearly know how these deeds will be,
whether well or badly we shall return, we sons of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: We do not yet clearly know how this business will turn out, or whether we sons of the Achaeans shall return well or badly.
sentences.n: Odysseus’ argument is that no one knows how the war will end, so abuse and talk of leaving are premature. οὐδέ τί πω is ‘nor yet at all’. ἴδμεν is the epic ἴσμεν ‘we know’ (οἶδα). ὅπως ἔσται τάδε ἔργα is an indirect question, ‘how these things will be’, and ἢ … ἦε … ‘whether … or’ gives the choice, εὖ ‘well’ or κακῶς ‘badly’. νοστήσομεν is the future of νοστέω ‘return home’.

sentences.t:
τὼ νῦν Ἀτρεΐδῃ Ἀγαμέμνονι ποιμένι λαῶν
ἧσαι ὀνειδίζων, ὅτι οἱ μάλα πολλὰ διδοῦσιν
ἥρωες Δαναοί· σὺ δὲ κερτομέων ἀγορεύεις.
sentences.tr:
tō nyn Atreïdēi Agamemnoni poimeni laōn
hēsai oneidizōn, hoti hoi mala polla didousin
hērōes Danaoi· sy de kertomeōn agoreueis.
sentences.l:
Therefore now at Atreus’-son Agamemnon, shepherd of the people,
you sit reproaching him, because very many things to him they give,
the Danaan heroes; but you, taunting, declare.
sentences.i: So now you sit there reproaching Agamemnon, son of Atreus, shepherd of the people, because the Danaan heroes give him a great many things; but you, taunting, speak out.
sentences.n: τὼ νῦν ‘therefore now’ draws the conclusion from 250–253. ἧσαι is the second person of ἧμαι ‘sit’, and ὀνειδίζων (from ὄνειδος ‘reproach’) takes the dative Ἀτρεΐδῃ Ἀγαμέμνονι. οἱ is ‘to him’, and διδοῦσιν is διδόασι ‘they give’. ἥρωες Δαναοί ‘Danaan heroes’: Odysseus names the givers, the whole army. κερτομέων is the participle of κερτομέω ‘taunt’ (compare κερτομίοισι at 1.539), and ἀγορεύεις ‘you declare’ in the assembly.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἔκ τοι ἐρέω, τὸ δὲ καὶ τετελεσμένον ἔσται·
sentences.tr: all’ ek toi ereō, to de kai tetelesmenon estai·
sentences.l: But I will speak out plainly to you, and this too shall be a thing fulfilled;
sentences.i: But I will tell you plainly, and this too will come true:
sentences.n: ἔκ … ἐρέω is tmesis for ἐξερέω ‘I will speak out’, with τοι ‘to you’. τὸ δὲ καὶ τετελεσμένον ἔσται, ‘and this too will be a thing fulfilled’, joins the perfect passive participle τετελεσμένον (τελέω ‘fulfil’) with ἔσται, a future perfect in sense. The Odyssey has the same line. Here it opens an oath.

sentences.t:
εἴ κ’ ἔτι σ’ ἀφραίνοντα κιχήσομαι ὥς νύ περ ὧδε,
μηκέτ’ ἔπειτ’ Ὀδυσῆϊ κάρη ὤμοισιν ἐπείη,
μηδ’ ἔτι Τηλεμάχοιο πατὴρ κεκλημένος εἴην,
sentences.tr:
ei k’ eti s’ aphrainonta kichēsomai hōs ny per hōde,
mēket’ epeit’ Odysēï karē ōmoisin epeiē,
mēd’ eti Tēlemachoio patēr keklēmenos eiēn,
sentences.l:
If I still find you, acting senselessly, just as now in this way,
then no longer upon Odysseus’ shoulders may there be a head,
and no longer called the father of Telemachus may I be,
sentences.i: If I still find you acting senselessly as you are now, then may Odysseus no longer have a head upon his shoulders, and may I no longer be called the father of Telemachus,
sentences.n: A solemn oath-wish: Odysseus stakes his head and his name as Telemachus’ father on the threat that follows. εἴ κ’ … κιχήσομαι is ‘if I find’ (κιχάνω); ἀφραίνοντα ‘acting senselessly’, from ἄφρων ‘without wits’; ὥς νύ περ ὧδε ‘just as now, in this way’. ἐπείη is the optative of ἔπειμι ‘be upon’ in a wish, and εἴην the optative of εἰμί. Odysseus names himself in the third person in 259, and speaks in the first person in 260. Τηλεμάχοιο is the epic genitive.

sentences.t:
εἰ μὴ ἐγώ σε λαβὼν ἀπὸ μὲν φίλα εἵματα δύσω,
χλαῖνάν τ’ ἠδὲ χιτῶνα, τά τ’ αἰδῶ ἀμφικαλύπτει,
αὐτὸν δὲ κλαίοντα θοὰς ἐπὶ νῆας ἀφήσω
πεπλήγων ἀγορῆθεν ἀεικέσσι πληγῇσιν.
sentences.tr:
ei mē egō se labōn apo men phila heimata dysō,
chlainan t’ ēde chitōna, ta t’ aidō amphikalyptei,
auton de klaionta thoas epi nēas aphēsō
peplēgōn agorēthen aeikessi plēgēisin.
sentences.l:
if I do not, taking you, strip your own clothes off you,
the cloak and the tunic, which enfold your shame,
and you yourself, weeping, to the swift ships send away
beating you from the assembly with unseemly blows.”
sentences.i: unless I seize you and strip off your own clothes, the cloak and the tunic that enfold your shame, and send you away weeping to the swift ships, beating you out of the assembly with unseemly blows.”
sentences.n: εἰ μὴ ἐγώ is the other half of the oath, ‘if I do not’: the penalty of 259–260 falls on Odysseus if he fails. ἀπὸ … δύσω is tmesis, ‘strip off’. φίλα εἵματα is ‘your own clothes’ (φίλος as ‘own’); χλαῖνα ‘cloak’, χιτών ‘tunic’; τά τ’ αἰδῶ ἀμφικαλύπτει ‘which enfold your shame’, that is, cover your nakedness. ἀφήσω is ‘I will send off’. πεπλήγων is the reduplicated aorist participle of πλήσσω ‘strike’; ἀγορῆθεν is ‘from the assembly’ (suffix -θεν); ἀεικέσσι is ‘unseemly’, with πληγῇσιν the epic dative plural.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη, σκήπτρῳ δὲ μετάφρενον ἠδὲ καὶ ὤμω
πλῆξεν·
sentences.tr:
hōs ar’ ephē, skēptrōi de metaphrenon ēde kai ōmō
plēxen·
sentences.l:
So then he spoke, and with the sceptre his back and both shoulders
struck;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and struck his back and both shoulders with the sceptre;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη ‘so then he spoke’ closes the speech, and the verb ‘struck’ waits for the start of the next line, after its objects. μετάφρενον is ‘the back’ (the place between the shoulders) and ὤμω the dual ‘both shoulders’; σκήπτρῳ is the dative of means. The sceptre taken at 186 is now used on a man, as 199 said it was on the common men.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἰδνώθη, θαλερὸν δέ οἱ ἔκπεσε δάκρυ·
sentences.tr: ho d’ idnōthē, thaleron de hoi ekpese dakry·
sentences.l: and he doubled over, and an abundant tear fell from him;
sentences.i: and he doubled over, and an abundant tear fell from him;
sentences.n: ὃ is ‘he’, Thersites. ἰδνώθη is the aorist passive of ἰδνόομαι ‘bend, double up’, in pain. θαλερὸν … δάκρυ is ‘an abundant tear’ (θαλερός ‘flourishing, abundant’); οἱ is ‘from him’, and ἔκπεσε ‘fell out’ (ἐκ and ἔπεσε).

sentences.t:
σμῶδιξ δ’ αἱματόεσσα μεταφρένου ἐξυπανέστη
σκήπτρου ὕπο χρυσέου·
sentences.tr:
smōdix d’ haimatoessa metaphrenou exypanestē
skēptrou hypo chryseou·
sentences.l:
and a bloody weal from his back stood up
under the golden sceptre;
sentences.i: and a bloody weal rose up on his back under the golden sceptre;
sentences.n: σμῶδιξ ‘weal’ is the raised mark of a blow, and αἱματόεσσα ‘bloody’ is the feminine of αἱματόεις. μεταφρένου ‘of the back’ says where the weal stands. ἐξυπανέστη is the aorist of ἐξυπανίσταμαι, ‘stood up out from under’, a verb with two prefixes. σκήπτρου ὕπο χρυσέου is ‘under the golden sceptre’, with ὕπο set after its noun (hence the accent) and χρυσέου the epic genitive of χρύσεος. The sceptre is the one Odysseus took at 186.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετο τάρβησέν τε,
ἀλγήσας δ’ ἀχρεῖον ἰδὼν ἀπομόρξατο δάκρυ.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ar’ hezeto tarbēsen te,
algēsas d’ achreion idōn apomorxato dakry.
sentences.l:
and he sat down, and was afraid,
and in pain, idly looking, wiped away a tear.
sentences.i: and he sat down in fear; in pain, with a vacant look, he wiped away a tear.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετο τάρβησέν τε is ‘and he sat down and was afraid’: ἕζετο from ἕζομαι ‘sit down’, τάρβησε the aorist of ταρβέω ‘be afraid’. ἀλγήσας is ‘having felt pain’ (ἀλγέω). ἀχρεῖον ἰδών: ἀχρεῖον ‘useless’ is a neuter used as an adverb, ‘to no purpose’, and the sense taken from the context is a blank, helpless look. ἀπομόρξατο is the aorist middle of ἀπομόργνυμι ‘wipe off’. The loud speaker is now silent.

sentences.t: οἳ δὲ καὶ ἀχνύμενοί περ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ ἡδὺ γέλασσαν·
sentences.tr: hoi de kai achnymenoi per ep’ autōi hēdy gelassan·
sentences.l: And they, even though grieving, at him sweetly laughed;
sentences.i: And they, though grieving, laughed with relish at him;
sentences.n: καὶ … περ is ‘even though’: ἀχνύμενοί περ ‘though they were grieving’, from ἄχνυμαι ‘grieve’. ἐπ’ αὐτῷ is ‘at him’, αὐτῷ here simply ‘him’. ἡδύ, the neuter of ἡδύς ‘sweet, pleasant’, is used as an adverb: they laughed with real pleasure. γέλασσαν is the aorist of γελάω with the epic σσ and no augment (= ἐγέλασαν).

sentences.t: ὧδε δέ τις εἴπεσκεν ἰδὼν ἐς πλησίον ἄλλον·
sentences.tr: hōde de tis eipesken idōn es plēsion allon·
sentences.l: And thus someone would say, looking to another close by:
sentences.i: And as each looked at the one beside him, he would say something like this:
sentences.n: ὧδε is ‘thus’ and τις ‘someone’; εἴπεσκεν is the iterative of εἶπον, ‘would say’: man after man made the same remark. ἰδὼν ἐς πλησίον ἄλλον is ‘looking to another near by’, πλησίον an adverb. The Odyssey has the same line.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι ἦ δὴ μυρί’ Ὀδυσσεὺς ἐσθλὰ ἔοργε
βουλάς τ’ ἐξάρχων ἀγαθὰς πόλεμόν τε κορύσσων·
sentences.tr:
ō popoi ē dē myri’ Odysseus esthla eorge
boulas t’ exarchōn agathas polemon te koryssōn·
sentences.l:
“Ah, truly, countless good things Odysseus has done,
leading off good counsels and arming war;
sentences.i: “Ah, Odysseus has truly done countless good things, taking the lead in good counsels and arming for war;
sentences.n: The speakers are unnamed soldiers, and the praise is for Odysseus. ὢ πόποι is the exclamation ‘Ah!’; ἦ δὴ is ‘truly now’; μυρί’ is μυρία ‘countless’; ἔοργε is the perfect of ἔρδω ‘do’, ‘has done’. ἐσθλά and ἀγαθάς are two words for ‘good’. ἐξάρχων is ‘leading off’. κορύσσων is the participle of κορύσσω ‘arm, put a helmet on’ (κόρυς ‘helmet’); with πόλεμον ‘war’ as its object the phrase is bold, something like ‘arming battle’, putting it in array.

sentences.t:
νῦν δὲ τόδε μέγ’ ἄριστον ἐν Ἀργείοισιν ἔρεξεν,
ὃς τὸν λωβητῆρα ἐπεσβόλον ἔσχ’ ἀγοράων.
sentences.tr:
nyn de tode meg’ ariston en Argeioisin erexen,
hos ton lōbētēra epesbolon esch’ agoraōn.
sentences.l:
but now this thing, by far the best, among the Argives he has done,
who the outrager, the word-flinger, has held back from the assemblies.
sentences.i: But now he has done by far the best thing among the Argives, in keeping this outrager, this word-flinger, out of the assemblies.
sentences.n: νῦν δὲ ‘but now’ turns from Odysseus’ old services to the latest. τόδε μέγ’ ἄριστον is ‘this, by far the best’, with ἔρεξεν the aorist of ῥέζω ‘did’. ὃς … ἔσχ’ is ‘he who has held back’, ἔσχε the aorist of ἔχω, with the genitive ἀγοράων ‘from the assemblies’ (epic -άων). τὸν points at Thersites: λωβητήρ, from λώβη ‘outrage’, is ‘the outrager’, and ἐπεσβόλον (ἔπος and βάλλω) ‘word-flinger’, one who throws words about without care.

sentences.t:
οὔ θήν μιν πάλιν αὖτις ἀνήσει θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ
νεικείειν βασιλῆας ὀνειδείοις ἐπέεσσιν.
sentences.tr:
ou thēn min palin autis anēsei thymos agēnōr
neikeiein basilēas oneideiois epeessin.
sentences.l:
Surely not again, once more, will his manly spirit urge him on
to rebuke kings with words of reproach.”
sentences.i: His proud spirit, I am sure, will not urge him on again to rebuke kings with words of reproach.”
sentences.n: οὔ θήν μιν is ‘surely not … him’: θήν is a particle of confident assertion, and μιν ‘him’ is Thersites. πάλιν αὖτις ‘back again’ puts ‘again’ twice. ἀνήσει is the future of ἀνίημι ‘send up, urge on’, with the infinitive νεικείειν (epic for νεικεῖν) ‘to rebuke’. θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ ‘proud spirit’ is a stock phrase, translated every time; ἀγήνωρ means ‘manly, proud’. ὀνειδείοις ἐπέεσσιν is ‘with words of reproach’.
